lessons.title: Life Insurance Premiums and ULIPs: When They Qualify and When to Avoid Them

children.text: More bad financial decisions in India are made in the name of 80C than for any other reason, and most of them are insurance policies. A relative who is an agent, a bank relationship manager in March, a brochure promising "tax saving plus guaranteed returns plus life cover". This lesson shows exactly which premiums qualify, how payouts are taxed, and the simple comparison that tells you whether a policy is protecting your family or just protecting someone's commission.

markDefs.definition: The guaranteed amount the insurer promises to pay on death, as stated in the policy document. It excludes bonuses and fund value.

children.text: The law does not want a savings product dressed up as insurance to get full insurance benefits. So for policies issued on or after 1 April 2012, the deduction is capped at 10% of the
. For policies issued between 1 April 2003 and 31 March 2012, the cap is 20%. For persons with disability or specified diseases, it is 15% for policies issued on or after 1 April 2013.

body.caption: Premium above the cap is not deductible, and the policy's maturity also loses its tax exemption.

body.title: Your Turn: Apply the Cap
body.prompt: Suresh, a shop owner in Madurai on the old regime, bought a savings plan in 2019 with a sum assured of ₹8,00,000 and an annual premium of ₹95,000. How much of the premium can he claim under Section 123 (80C) this year?
body.explanation: The policy was issued after 1 April 2012, so the cap is 10% of ₹8,00,000 = ₹80,000. The remaining ₹15,000 is not deductible. Worse, because the premium exceeds 10% of the sum assured, the maturity amount will not be tax-free either.

children.text: The exemption for life insurance payouts, Section 10(10D) under the 1961 Act, now sits in Schedule II (Sr. No. 2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The conditions carried over unchanged. Because it is an exemption, not a deduction, it applies under both regimes.

cards.term: Maturity: premium above 10% of sum assured
cards.definition: Taxable. For traditional policies, the gain is taxed as income at your slab.

cards.term: Traditional policies issued on or after 1 April 2023
cards.definition: Maturity is taxable if total yearly premium across such policies exceeds ₹5 lakh.

cards.term: ULIPs issued on or after 1 February 2021
cards.definition: Maturity is taxable if total yearly ULIP premium exceeds ₹2.5 lakh. Gains are taxed as capital gains, at 12.5% under Section 198 (112A) if held over a year.
Surrender a traditional policy within 2 years, or a ULIP within 5 years, and all 80C deductions claimed on it are added back to your income.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: If you surrender a ULIP within ___ years, the 80C deductions you claimed on its premiums are reversed.
body.explanation: ULIPs carry a 5-year lock-in. For traditional policies, the clawback applies if premiums stop within 2 years.

body.text: Insurance and investment are two different jobs. Products that try to do both usually do both badly.

children.text: Ramesh, 30, a government school teacher in Lucknow on the old regime, is offered an endowment plan: ₹50,000 a year for 20 years, sum assured ₹5 lakh, with an illustrated maturity of ₹16.5 lakh including bonuses. The alternative is to split the same ₹50,000: about ₹9,000 for a ₹1 crore term plan and ₹41,000 into PPF or ELSS. Both routes use the same ₹50,000 of his 80C limit.

body.title: What ₹50,000 a year becomes after 20 years

body.label: Cover Ramesh gives up with the endowment
body.context: ₹5 lakh of cover against ₹1 crore, for the same premium outlay and the same 80C deduction. If he dies in year 5, his family gets ₹5 lakh plus bonuses instead of ₹1 crore.

body.title: 80C Check
body.question: Ramesh chooses the term plan plus PPF route instead of the endowment. What happens to his Section 123 (80C) deduction?
options: It falls to ₹9,000, since only the term premium is insurance
It stays at ₹50,000, since both the term premium and PPF deposit qualify
It falls to ₹41,000, since term plans do not qualify
It rises to ₹1,00,000, since each product has its own limit
body.explanation: Term premiums and PPF deposits both qualify under Section 123 (80C). The split costs Ramesh nothing in deductions, gives him 20 times the cover, and very likely more money at the end.

children.text: ULIPs: Better Than They Were, Still Not Simple

body.title: ULIP vs term plan plus ELSS

columns.label: ULIP
points: Premium split between life cover and market-linked funds
Charges: premium allocation, mortality, policy administration and fund management (capped at 1.35% a year)
Cover is usually 10 times the annual premium, often too low for a family
Tax-free maturity only if yearly premium is ₹2.5 lakh or less and within 10% of sum assured
Free switches between equity and debt funds inside the policy

columns.label: Term plan + ELSS
points: Cover and investment are separate and transparent
Term premium buys pure cover; ELSS charges only an expense ratio
Cover sized to your actual need, such as ₹1 crore or more
ELSS gains taxed at 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh a year
Switching funds is a redemption, which can trigger capital gains tax

body.text: Already stuck with a poor policy? Do not surrender it in a panic. Check three things first: whether you are past the 2-year (traditional) or 5-year (ULIP) clawback window, the surrender value versus the paid-up value if you simply stop paying, and what the remaining premiums would earn elsewhere. For traditional policies issued on or after 1 October 2024, IRDAI's special surrender value rules pay a meaningful amount even after just one year of premiums.

body.title: Scenario: The Family Agent
body.scenario: Kavitha, 27, is a software tester in Coimbatore earning ₹9,00,000 a year. Her aunt, an insurance agent, suggests a money-back plan at ₹1,00,000 a year for 15 years, pitched as 'tax saving, guaranteed returns and life cover in one'. Kavitha is on the new regime. Her parents depend partly on her income. She also holds an endowment policy her father bought for her in 2021, with a ₹40,000 yearly premium and ₹4 lakh sum assured.
body.prompt: Should Kavitha buy the money-back plan? What should she do about her existing policy and her real insurance need?
body.modelAnswer: She should not buy it. First, she is on the new regime, where ₹1,00,000 of insurance premium earns no deduction at all. At a ₹9 lakh salary, the new regime gives her zero tax anyway because of the ₹12 lakh rebate. Second, money-back and endowment plans typically return around 4% to 6% a year, and the cover is small relative to the premium. Her real need is protection for dependent parents: a ₹1 crore term plan at her age costs roughly ₹8,500 to ₹9,000 a year, now with no GST. For her 2021 endowment: it is past the 2-year window, so stopping would not trigger any clawback, and she is on the new regime anyway. She should ask the insurer for both the surrender value and the paid-up value, and compare continuing ₹40,000 a year for the remaining term against investing that amount in PPF or an index fund. Her premium is exactly 10% of the sum assured, so the maturity stays tax-free if she continues. Whatever she decides, she should not treat the ₹4 lakh cover as adequate protection.

body.title: Audit Your Existing Policies
steps: List every policy: insurer, type, start date, sum assured, annual premium and maturity date
Check each premium against 10% of sum assured (20% for pre-April 2012 policies)
Add up your total life cover and compare it with about 10 to 15 times your yearly income
Note which policies are still inside the 2-year (traditional) or 5-year (ULIP) clawback window
Request surrender and paid-up values in writing for any policy you are considering stopping
If your cover is short, buy a term plan before stopping any existing policy
Keep premium receipts only for policies on self, spouse or children as 80C proof

points: Life insurance premiums on self, spouse or children qualify under Section 123 (80C), capped at 10% of sum assured for policies from April 2012.
The payout exemption (10(10D) under the 1961 Act) is now Schedule II, Sr. No. 2, and applies under both regimes.
Death benefits are always tax-free; maturity loses its exemption above the 10% rule, ₹5 lakh premium for newer traditional plans or ₹2.5 lakh for newer ULIPs.
Stopping a traditional policy within 2 years, or a ULIP within 5, reverses past 80C deductions.
A term plan plus PPF or ELSS usually gives far more cover and a better return than an endowment, for the same 80C deduction.
Audit existing policies calmly before surrendering, and secure adequate term cover first.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not insurance, tax or investment advice, and does not recommend any specific insurer or policy. Premium estimates and policy returns are illustrative; actual figures depend on age, health, insurer and plan terms. Read the policy document and benefit illustration carefully, and consult a qualified professional before buying or surrendering any policy.
